boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Ratkau entry (capitulation, 7 November 1806) in cohort v1's fourth-coalition 1806 group: General Blücher's corps from the night of 6 to 7 November at Ratkau to its capitulation there and its defile at noon. The fight for Lübeck on 6 November (B376a), with Majors Ende's and Witzleben's detachments taken that day, is not counted here. The surprise of Schwartau in the night is context: its prisoners, most of the regiment Kunheim, are not counted here, and whether they belong with B376a is left to that entry. The 29th Bulletin's 16,000 prisoners cover both days and are not added. Travemünde's surrender on 8 November and General Pelet's capitulation of 11 and 12 November are outside this entry. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) as about 40,000 men under Marshals Bernadotte and Soult, and side B (Prussian) as 9,000 Prussians, of whom about 4,000 cavalry, under Lieutenant General von Blücher; besides the regimental guns, 16 guns fell to the French. By his stated rule his figures are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. Höpfner and the French documents give other figures (claims side-b-strength, side-b-strength-french, side-a-strength). English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the heading and entry: '1806 7/11. capitulation of Ratkau'; 'the French (about 40,000 men) under Marshals Bernadotte and Soult force 9,000 men of Prussians (of whom about 4,000 men cavalry) under Lieutenant General von Blücher to capitulate, after which the corps went into captivity and the officers were released on parole'; 'besides the regimental guns, 16 more guns became the booty of the French'.

citations.quote: 1806 7./11. KAPITULATION von Ratkau

Die Franzosen (ca. 40.000 M.) unter den Marschällen Bernadotte und Soult zwingen 9.000 M. Preußen (wov. ca. 4.000 M. Kavallerie) unter Gen.-Lt. von Blücher zur Kapitulation, wonach das Korps in Kriegsgefangenschaft geriet, die Offiziere gegen Ehrenwort entlassen wurden.
Außer den Regimentskanonen wurden noch 16 Geschütze die Beute der Franzosen.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian) in Höpfner: General Blücher's corps had only about 8000 men left, and the artillery and the infantry, except the regiment Borcke and the grenadier battalion Gaudi, were without ammunition. Citing the work 'Operationsplan der preußisch-sächsischen Armee im Jahre 1806' by C. v. W., Höpfner gives the infantry still taken prisoner by the capitulation at Ratkau as 4050 men and the cavalry as 3760, a figure he calls only approximate because returns could not be made after the preceding events; 16 guns, without the regimental cannon, were handed over.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images of pp. 303 and 305; the 3760 was checked on a full-resolution crop (the OCR reads 3700). The corps was brought from the retreat, so the claim is tagged inherited. 4050 and 3760 make 7810 (our arithmetic), close to Höpfner's about 8000; the two counts are kept as given. General Blücher is named in the sentence that follows the state of the corps. English renderings (ours): 'ahead, in Schwartau and Lübeck, the enemy; on the right the Danish border; on the left the Trave, held by the enemy; behind, the sea and the enemy in Travemünde; and with this the artillery and the infantry, except the regiment Borcke and the grenadier battalion Gaudi, without ammunition, the men without bread, the horses without forage, both exhausted and shaken to the utmost, and only about 8000 men left'; 'nevertheless General Blücher had Marshal Bernadotte told through the parlementaire that his position was not yet as bad as he, the marshal, might think, that he would therefore never accept a capitulation unless it were very honourable; for the rest one must wait for the day to agree on what followed'; 'according to the work "Plan of operations of the Prusso-Saxon army in the year 1806 by C. v. W.", the infantry still taken prisoner by the capitulation at Ratkau is reckoned at 4050 men, the cavalry at 3760 men, but this is only an approximate figure, since after the preceding events the submission of returns had been impossible'; 'of guns, without the regimental cannon, 16 more were handed over'.

claims.value: Side A (French): Bodart gives about 40,000 under Bernadotte and Soult. The Grand Duke of Berg wrote that Blücher's corps surrendered to the 3 corps gathered at Lübeck, and Bernadotte authorised Rivaud and Tilly to accept the capitulation in the name of the 3 corps of the Grande Armée. The 29th Bulletin has the Grand Duke surround the enemy near Schwartau before daylight on the 7th with Lasalle's brigade and d'Hautpoul's cuirassier division. In Höpfner, Generals Tilly and Rivaud put to Blücher the impossibility of resisting 80,000 men any longer. No passage read gives a count of the French troops present.
claims.rationale: Bodart from the frame transcription, the rest read from the page images. The corps were brought up by the pursuit, so the claim is tagged inherited. claims.value: Bernadotte wrote on 8 November that the morning before, as he was preparing to attack the rest of the enemy gathered at Ratkau, Blücher asked to capitulate, and that after taking the Grand Duke of Berg's opinion he authorised Generals Rivaud and Tilly, who faced the enemy, to accept the capitulation in the name of the 3 corps. Belliard wrote that the Prince had sent a dragoon officer to summon Blücher to surrender and lay down his arms, and that Blücher had accepted the conditions when Rivaud and Tilly reached the advance guard and made the capitulation with him. In Höpfner a dragoon officer summoned Blücher in the Grand Duke of Berg's name towards morning; at daybreak the leader of the French advance guard claimed to have orders to attack, and Tilly and Rivaud would stop the attack only if Blücher capitulated at once on Bernadotte's terms. The two generals came back from the field before Ratkau saying that, having met the Grand Duke there, the draft had to be changed, since all 3 corps had taken part.
claims.rationale: Side A's letters and side B's history, read from the page images. The summons and the terms were decided at the engagement by side A's commanders, so the claim is tagged commander-created. Belliard's 'Prince' is not named in the passage read; Höpfner has the dragoon officer's summons made in the Grand Duke of Berg's name. English renderings (ours): 'Marshal Bernadotte to the Emperor. Lübeck, 8 November 1806'; 'I hasten today to announce to Your Majesty that yesterday morning, as I was preparing to attack the rest of the enemy troops gathered at Ratkau, General Blücher asked me to capitulate'; 'after taking the opinion of His Highness the Grand Duke of Berg, I authorised Generals Rivaud and Tilly, who were facing them, to accept in the name of the 3 corps of the Grande Armée the capitulation, a copy of which I send Your Majesty; 27 battalions and 52 squadrons laid down their arms'; 'General Belliard to the major general. Lübeck, 7 November 1806'; 'the Prince sent an officer of dragoons to summon General Blücher to surrender with his corps and lay down his arms'; 'General Blücher had accepted the conditions when Generals Rivaud and Tilly arrived at the advance guard and made a capitulation with General Blücher'; Höpfner, 'towards the morning of 7 November a dragoon officer also arrived in Ratkau, who summoned General Blücher to surrender in the name of the Grand Duke of Berg'; 'the leader of the enemy advance guard, however, asserted that he had the order to attack'; 'the Prussian officer had himself taken to Generals Tilly and Rivaud, who would stop the attack only if General Blücher capitulated at once, as Marshal Bernadotte offered the following terms: to lay down their arms and surrender as prisoners of war, but keep all their property'; 'the two French generals went with the draft capitulation to the field in front of Ratkau, where Marshal Bernadotte was supposed to be, but soon came back and remarked that they had met the Grand Duke of Berg there, and that this made a change necessary, since all 3 corps had taken part in the happy result'.

claims.value: Höpfner: General Blücher gave up, reluctantly, the plan of a night attack on Lübeck and ordered his troops to assemble between Ivendorf and Travemünde at 9 the next morning. Through the parlementaire he had Bernadotte told that he would never accept a capitulation that was not very honourable. Summoned towards morning, he sent officers to all his troops with orders to halt and not fire on the enemy, and answered the Grand Duke of Berg that he had entered into negotiations with Bernadotte. Captain Müffling drafted a capitulation whose preamble said that Blücher lacked bread, forage and ammunition; when the French generals reported that the Grand Duke of Berg held it unusual to state reasons in a capitulation, Blücher held that his own honour and the corps's required them, and wrote under the capitulation: 'I capitulate because I have no bread and no ammunition.'
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images of pp. 297 and 303-305. These were Blücher's decisions at the engagement, so the claim is tagged commander-created. Where the passage says only 'the General', the claim cites the sentence before it that names Blücher. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'General Blücher sent Lieutenant Phull as parlementaire to Marshal Bernadotte and asked for good treatment of the prisoners'; 'in view of the disproportion that had arisen between infantry and artillery and the cavalry, the General decided, though only with difficulty, to give up the plan of a night attack on Lübeck'; 'the order was therefore sent to all troops to assemble the next morning at 9 o'clock between Ivendorf and Travemünde'; 'nevertheless General Blücher had Marshal Bernadotte told through the parlementaire that his position was not yet as bad as he, the marshal, might think, that he would therefore never accept a capitulation unless it were very honourable; for the rest one must wait for the day to agree on what followed'; 'the General now sent officers to all troops with the order to stand still and not to fire on the enemy, and then had the Grand Duke of Berg answered, on the summons given, that he had entered into negotiations with Marshal Bernadotte, with whom he had already been fighting for 8 days'; 'Captain Müffling now had to draw up a capitulation, which said in its preamble: "As General Blücher lacks bread, forage and ammunition, he accepts the capitulation that Marshal Prince of Ponte-Corvo has had offered to him"'; 'the Grand Duke had also remarked that it was not customary to state in capitulations the reason why one had entered into them'; 'General Blücher declared, however, that it was necessary for his own honour and that of the corps that the reasons that decided him to capitulate be known'; 'General Blücher now wrote under the capitulation: "I capitulate because I have no bread and no ammunition." Blücher'.

claims.value: Bodart records the capitulation of Ratkau on 7 November: the corps went into captivity and the officers were released on parole. The capitulation Foucart prints, done at 'Ratzkaw' on 7 November and signed by Blücher and Rivaud, makes all the troops under Blücher prisoners of war; arms, horses, guns and munitions were to be handed over at once; officers kept their arms, horses and baggage and the men their packs; officers were prisoners on parole; the military chest and all the funds of His Prussian Majesty at Blücher's disposal were to be handed over; and the corps was to defile at noon with the honours of war and lay down its arms after passing the French left. The Grand Duke of Berg reported that morning that the corps had surrendered and would defile within the hour; Belliard, that it defiled at noon. Höpfner: the troops defiled past the French army at noon, and a fair number of officers escaped through Danish territory.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome with the capitulation's text and the reports, read from the page images (Bodart's from the frame transcription); no source read gives a different result. Foucart prints the capitulation as an extract in a footnote to Belliard's letter; article 6 is not restated. The 29th Bulletin calls it the capitulation of Schwartau. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; article 1, 'the troops under the orders of His Excellency General de Blücher, cavalry, infantry and artillery and every detachment forming part of his command, shall be prisoners of war'; article 2, 'the arms, horses, cannon and munitions of every kind shall be handed over to the French army at once'; article 3, 'the officers of every rank, including the cadets, shall keep their arms, horses and baggage; the non-commissioned officers and soldiers shall keep their packs and valises'; article 4, 'the officers surrender as prisoners on parole and undertake to go to the place that will be indicated to them'; article 5, 'the military chest and all the funds belonging to His Prussian Majesty that are at the disposal of General de Blücher shall be handed over to the French army'; article 7, 'the corps of His Excellency General de Blücher shall defile today at noon, with the honours of war, before the French army with its arms, cannon, flags and standards unfurled. It shall lay down its arms after it has passed the left of the French army'; 'done in duplicate at Ratzkaw, 7 November 1806'; 'Lieutenant General de Blücher'; 'General of Division Rivaud'; 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. Behind Schwartau, 7 November 1806, half past ten in the morning'; 'I hasten to announce to Your Majesty that General Blücher's corps surrendered this morning to the 3 corps that are gathered at Lübeck'; 'it will defile in an hour before them'; 'General Belliard to the major general. Lübeck, 7 November 1806'; 'at noon the column defiled before His Majesty's troops and 27 battalions and 52 squadrons laid down their arms'; '29th Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 9 November 1806'; 'the fourth by the capitulation of Schwartau'; Höpfner, 'at noon the Blücher troops defiled past the French army'; 'a fair number of officers managed to save themselves through Danish territory and escape captivity'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian) lost the corps that capitulated. Höpfner: 4050 infantry and 3760 cavalry taken prisoner by the capitulation, by C. v. W.'s approximate reckoning, and 16 guns besides the regimental cannon. Bodart: 9,000 Prussians, of whom about 4,000 cavalry, into captivity, and 16 guns besides the regimental guns. Belliard: 27 battalions and 52 squadrons laid down their arms, the prisoners estimated at 12 or 15,000. Bernadotte: 27 battalions and 52 squadrons, and enemy flags, 15 of them won on the field of battle; his letter, which also covers the 6th, does not say how many came from the capitulation. Soult: 53 squadrons, more than 6,000 horses. The 29th Bulletin gives 16,000 prisoners, among them 4,000 cavalry, for 'these 2 days' together, the day at Lübeck and the capitulation, and 4,000 prisoners for the day at Lübeck alone.
claims.rationale: Separate accounts read from the page images (Bodart's from the frame transcription), not combined. The Bulletin's 16,000 covers Lübeck and Ratkau together and is not this entry's figure; the 4,000 it gives for Lübeck belong to B376a. Bodart's 16 guns are Höpfner's; which source Bodart used was not checked. Before the capitulation, in the night surprise of Schwartau, most of the regiment Kunheim was captured at the bridge (Höpfner); that loss is not counted here (see the boundary note). English renderings (ours): 'according to the work "Plan of operations of the Prusso-Saxon army in the year 1806 by C. v. W.", the infantry still taken prisoner by the capitulation at Ratkau is reckoned at 4050 men, the cavalry at 3760 men, but this is only an approximate figure, since after the preceding events the submission of returns had been impossible'; 'of guns, without the regimental cannon, 16 more were handed over'; Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'General Belliard to the major general. Lübeck, 7 November 1806'; 'at noon the column defiled before His Majesty's troops and 27 battalions and 52 squadrons laid down their arms'; 'the number of prisoners is estimated at 12 or 15,000'; 'Marshal Bernadotte to the Emperor. Lübeck, 8 November 1806'; 'I have sent the major general the details of the successes won on the day of the 6th over the Prussian troops and the Swedish troops'; 'after taking the opinion of His Highness the Grand Duke of Berg, I authorised Generals Rivaud and Tilly, who were facing them, to accept in the name of the 3 corps of the Grande Armée the capitulation, a copy of which I send Your Majesty; 27 battalions and 52 squadrons laid down their arms'; 'tomorrow, Sire, I shall have the honour of sending Your Majesty the enemy flags, of which 15 were won on the field of battle'; 'Marshal Soult to the Emperor. claims.value: Bodart places Ratkau as a village 8 km north of Lübeck. Höpfner: the country around Ratkau and Schwartau was unsuited to cavalry movements in large bodies, and the road and fields as far as Travemünde were enclosed by hedges; north of Travemünde there was said to be a plain, with old works behind which infantry could hold. On the road to Schwartau the way was blocked by vehicles and by the exhausted infantry lying on it. Blücher's corps had the enemy ahead in Schwartau and Lübeck, the Danish border on its right, the Trave held by the enemy on its left, and the sea and, as it believed, the enemy in Travemünde behind it.
claims.rationale: Bodart's locator and side B's history, read from the page images. The enemy in Travemünde was the corps's belief at the time; Höpfner says it was learned after the capitulation that Travemünde had not been given up (claim side-b-information). English renderings (ours): Bodart, '(village in Germany, 8 km north of Lübeck)'; Höpfner, as in claim side-b-strength for the state of the corps and Blücher's reply; 'the country around Ratkau and Schwartau was not suited to cavalry movements on a large scale, the road and the fields as far as Travemünde were enclosed with hedges; on the other hand north of Travemünde there was said to be a plain, and the old works of the place to be in a state that infantry could hold behind them'; 'towards Schwartau the road was jammed by vehicles, or blocked by the exhausted infantry encamped on it'; 'ahead, in Schwartau and Lübeck, the enemy; on the right the Danish border; on the left the Trave, held by the enemy; behind, the sea and the enemy in Travemünde; and with this the artillery and the infantry, except the regiment Borcke and the grenadier battalion Gaudi, without ammunition, the men without bread, the horses without forage, both exhausted and shaken to the utmost, and only about 8000 men left'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian): Höpfner says the artillery and the infantry, except the regiment Borcke and the grenadier battalion Gaudi, were without ammunition, the men without bread and the horses without forage, both exhausted and shaken to the utmost; the capitulation's draft preamble gave Blücher's want of bread, forage and ammunition as its reason, and Blücher wrote that he capitulated because he had no bread and no ammunition. Side A (French): Bernadotte asked the Emperor to let the 1st corps rest for a dozen days to restore men and horses, gather stragglers and above all restore some discipline.
claims.rationale: Side B's history and side A's letter, read from the page images. The state of both forces was brought from the pursuit, so the claim is tagged inherited. claims.value: Höpfner: while orders for the next day were being given at Ratkau, news came that the enemy had surprised Schwartau and taken the troops there. The fold-out situation tables in Foucart's annexes (after p. 939), among them one the OCR heads '... de la réserve. Situation au 8 novembre', could give part of it; they were not read.

Disputes kept as separate claims: side B's strength (about 8000 left, Höpfner, and C. v. W.'s 4050 infantry and 3760 cavalry, 7810 by our arithmetic; 9,000 with about 4,000 cavalry, Bodart; 12 or 15,000 prisoners, Belliard; the Bulletin's 16,000 with 4,000 cavalry for 6 and 7 November together); the squadrons (52, Belliard and Bernadotte; 53 with more than 6,000 horses, Soult); side A (about 40,000, Bodart; the 80,000 of the French generals, Höpfner); who summoned Blücher (a dragoon officer sent by the Prince, Belliard; in the Grand Duke of Berg's name, Höpfner) and on whose authority the capitulation was accepted (Bernadotte's, by his letter; the draft changed because all 3 corps had taken part, Höpfner); the name of the capitulation (Ratkau, Bodart and Höpfner; 'Ratzkaw' in its text; Schwartau, the 29th Bulletin).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked, though his 16 guns besides the regimental guns are Höpfner's); Foucart, t. II (the French side's documents: the Grand Duke of Berg's letter of 7 November, Belliard's letter with the capitulation's extract, Bernadotte's and Soult's letters of 8 November and the 29th Bulletin, from the page images); Höpfner, Bd. 2, 2nd edition (the Prussian side's history; by the preface of his first volume the work rests chiefly on the records of the judicial inquiries held after the war; for the prisoners he cites the work by C. v. W., and the Ratkau passage names no other source).
